title: Skidmore v. Swift & Co. (1944)
summary: An agency’s informed interpretation can persuade a court through its reasoning, experience, and consistency. In the employees’ waiting-time dispute, that respect did not determine compensation automatically.
notes: Justice Jackson wrote for a unanimous Court; the classic formulation is that the weight of an agency judgment 'will depend upon the thoroughness evident in its consideration, the validity of its reasoning, its consistency with earlier and later pronouncements, and all those factors which give it power to persuade, if lacking power to control.'.

sections.Parties: Employees of Swift & Company’s packing plant sought overtime compensation under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Swift disputed whether their inactive overnight duty counted as work. The federal Wage and Hour Administrator participated through an amicus brief, offering the enforcement agency’s interpretation; the Administrator was not the adjudicator of the employees’ private claim. (Packet printed 930–931.)
sections.Material Facts:
The employees’ oral agreement required them to remain in the plant’s fire hall, or within hailing distance, for several nights each week so that they could answer alarms. No fires occurred during the relevant period and alarms were rare. Their legal claim therefore turned on the restrictions created by being on call, even when they performed little active labor. (Printed 930.)

The Administrator’s interpretive bulletin treated inactive-duty problems flexibly. In the amicus submission, the Administrator proposed excluding these employees’ sleeping and eating time because interruptions were rare and the activities could be pursued comfortably. The remaining on-call time could count because the record did not establish that the men were free to spend it as they would otherwise have chosen. These were the Administrator’s proposed distinctions, whose persuasive force the Court evaluated. (Printed 931.)
sections.Procedural History: The packet describes the employees’ private overtime suit and reproduces the Court’s discussion of the Administrator’s views, but omits the complete lower-court history and final disposition. The following procedural supplement comes from the official report, 323 U.S. 134, 135–137, 140: the district court denied recovery, the Fifth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court reversed and remanded because the trial court’s inquiry had been constrained by its erroneous assumption that waiting time could not be work. The Court did not award a specified amount of overtime pay.
sections.Issue: What weight should a court deciding a private Fair Labor Standards Act claim give the Administrator’s interpretation of compensable waiting time, when Congress assigned the courts initial responsibility for resolving such claims and the Administrator’s views came from bulletins, informal rulings, and an amicus brief? (Printed 930–932.)
sections.Holding: The Administrator’s views supplied informed guidance whose weight depended on their persuasive qualities. They did not bind the court merely because the Administrator issued them. The Court identified thorough consideration, valid reasoning, consistency with earlier and later pronouncements, and other indicia of persuasion as relevant factors. (Printed 932.) The official-report procedural supplement confirms reversal and remand for a proper, fact-specific inquiry, rather than a conclusive award for all overnight hours.
sections.Reasoning:
Congress had given the Administrator investigatory and enforcement duties that produced knowledge of industrial practices beyond what a judge would ordinarily acquire from one lawsuit. The agency also needed workable standards to decide when to seek injunctions. Courts and litigants could use that accumulated experience, and unwarranted divergence between public enforcement and private rights would impair administration. (Printed 930–932.)

Those reasons for respect coexisted with independent judicial responsibility. The Administrator had not conducted an adversarial hearing resolving these employees’ claim, and Congress had not made his opinions authoritative judicial precedents. Their nonadversarial origin did not eliminate their value, but their usefulness depended on the quality of their analysis and fit with the actual facts. The Administrator’s distinction between sleeping or eating and other restricted time demonstrated how specialized experience could inform that inquiry. (Printed 931–932.)
